cards.headline: At least 25 people killed in Saudi airstrikes, Houthi-linked media report

pages.text: Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen report that at least 25 people, including women and children, were killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia. A spokesman for the Houthi-run Health Ministry told AP that the strikes hit homes in a village near Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, also injuring approximately 30 others. Live video footage from the Houthi-run television station Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies, including those of young children, from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town east of Sanaa. The station also broadcast footage of injured people being carried to hospitals on stretchers. The Saba news agency, also run by the Houthis, attributed the attack to Saudi Arabia. There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The escalation follows a period of dormant conflict that reignited due to the Iran war. A truce began to fail after Saudi Arabia struck the Houthi-controlled airport in Sanaa to prevent an Iranian landing plan. In response, the Tehran-backed Houthis targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia and began hitting Saudi ships in the Red Sea. Major fighting has since resumed between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed in a statement that the group carried out six military operations using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones in retaliation for Saudi strikes on civilians in Taiz and Bani Hashish. Saree stated the first operation targeted Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, along with Aramco oil storage tanks and a distillation tower in the Saudi capital, claiming the attack successfully achieved its objective.

Saree reported that a second operation targeted Aramco facilities in Khurais, a major oil-producing area in eastern Saudi Arabia, while a third targeted Pumping Station No. 8 in the Dawadmi area. Three other operations were directed at Saudi military personnel, including an attack on a Saudi National Guard camp in Najran where Saree claimed there were a large number of casualties. Two additional operations were reported in Yemen's Marib and Al-Jawf regions, which Saree said struck Saudi troop concentrations. In a separate post on X, Saree claimed Saudi forces conducted 105 airstrikes and missile attacks over a 24-hour period, hitting areas including Sanaa, Al-Jawf, Taiz, Amran, Hajjah, Saada, Marib, and Lahj. He claimed these attacks brought the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the latest escalation began to 4,369. Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces stated they repelled Houthi military movements in the Seventh Military Region on the northern front of Marib Governorate, claiming to have destroyed combat equipment and neutralized groups deployed by the Houthis.

cards.headline: U.S. sanctions eight Canadian currency-exchange businesses for allegedly aiding Iran and a drug trafficking suspect

pages.text: The United States Department of the Treasury has announced sanctions against eight Canadian currency-exchange businesses in Ontario and British Columbia. The U.S. government accuses these businesses of helping Iranian entities evade financial sanctions and, in several instances, assisting the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring. According to the Treasury, some of these businesses helped launder proceeds of crime by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, such as cryptocurrency. The sanctions effectively cut the firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets they may hold in the United States and banning any transactions with American people or entities.

The Treasury stated the crackdown is part of an effort to sever economic lifelines for the Iranian regime and its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada. U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent said in a statement that Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators providing sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies. The Treasury also noted that in several cases, the sanctioned businesses changed their names and addresses to avoid detection. In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions, which allow the government to impose penalties on entities and countries that maintain business connections with Iran.

The Treasury identified that three of the sanctioned businesses helped Ryan Wedding, an Olympian described as an alleged drug kingpin, hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. The Treasury reported that these companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January. The U.S. government's actions follow an expansion of secondary sanctions intended to increase economic pressure on Tehran.

cards.headline: Kyiv faces blackouts and water shortages after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure

pages.text: Kyiv, Ukraine, is experiencing serious difficulties with electricity, water, and heat supplies following an overnight attack by Russia on energy infrastructure and a bridge over the Dnipro River. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of attempting to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout.” The strikes injured five people, including a 14-year-old girl. The attacks follow a week of day-long power cuts and water supply interruptions for Kyiv residents. The Northern Bridge, described as a key transport artery, was closed while workers repaired power lines and damage to the road surface.

Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in the attack targeting Kyiv and surrounding regions. The strikes hit electricity substations in five regions, including one substation that connects two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. Ukrainian officials stated that the Kremlin's goal is to freeze civilians into submission during the winter months, an act they characterized as a war crime. Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress—which was won by Democrats in the midterm elections—for increased bilateral support, stating, “Ukraine must not be left alone.”

The bombardment occurs as negotiators from Russia, Ukraine, and the US are scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on November 10, 2026, for talks aimed at ending the war. This trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind since February. Zelenskyy noted that Moscow's preparations for these peace talks involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles. Ukrainian officials expressed little confidence that the US-backed talks will yield concrete results.

cards.headline: Explosions reported in Strait of Hormuz as Iran reviews Qatari de-escalation proposals

pages.text: Explosions have been heard on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, and tankers in the strategic waterway have caught fire after hitting mines. This occurs as Iran reviews mediation proposals presented by Qatar intended to address differences with the United States regarding Tehran's nuclear program. On November 6, 2026, US President Donald Trump discussed these mediation efforts in a call with Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani. The emir's office stated the two discussed efforts to reach a comprehensive agreement to end the crisis and achieve regional security and stability, though the specific contents of the call were not revealed. The Associated Press reported that these proposals could lead to indirect talks on Iran's atomic activities, a central issue for President Trump in efforts to end the more than eight-month-old war. However, one official stated that Iranians remain unwilling to negotiate over atomic activities until the US agrees to several conditions. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard announced it has lifted a self-imposed 2,000-kilometre limit on the range of its ballistic missiles. On November 6, 2026, President Trump also stated that the US military had carried out new, limited strikes against an Iranian air defence system, which he described to reporters as “minor.”

cards.headline: Six killed and 16 wounded after gunman opens fire in Kraków market square

pages.text: A gunman opened fire with an automatic weapon in the main market square of Kraków, Poland, killing six people and wounding 16 others. Polish defense minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz described the shooting as an “act of terror” on the people of the city. The attack occurred at approximately 3pm, when a tram driver reported that a man in a moving car shot at his vehicle near the square, shattering the cabin window, according to the Kraków municipal transport company. Following the shooting, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk stated that two women and one man were found dead in the suspect’s home, whom he noted were most likely members of the suspect's family.

Polish police reported that the six people killed in the market square included four women and two men. Among the deceased was a British citizen. Of the fatalities, three were identified as Polish women, while the remaining two victims had not been identified. The 16 wounded individuals included two police officers; one officer is in serious condition after being shot three times during an exchange of fire with the alleged attacker. A Polish government spokesperson stated that the foreign nationals among the wounded were from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal, and Russia.

The suspect is a 25-year-old Polish citizen. At a news conference, Polish interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views. Kraków is Poland’s second-largest city and receives approximately 15 million visitors a year, many of whom pass through the main square.

cards.headline: Bulk carrier involved in incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman

pages.text: A bulk carrier was involved in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). The incident occurred approximately 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates. At the time of the UKMTO report, the status of the vessel’s crew, the extent of any damage, and the possible environmental impact were unknown. UKMTO, a maritime security agency, cited military authorities as its source, stating that authorities had been notified and investigations were ongoing. The agency advised vessels in the area to monitor maritime security information and remain aware of the evolving operational environment.

This incident marks the sixth vessel involved in reported attacks or security incidents across the Gulf of Oman-Strait of Hormuz corridor. These reports from UKMTO have occurred since Nov. 1 and have involved tankers, a traditional sailing vessel, and other commercial shipping. On Nov. 5, 2026, the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Velos Sapphire was sailing to Bahrain empty of cargo when an explosion, likely caused by an unidentified projectile that struck the vessel’s port quarter and sparked a fire, occurred, according to Velos Tankers. The owner of the Greek-owned oil tanker reported that a seafarer was killed in an apparent missile attack in the Gulf. Separately, on Nov. 5, 2026, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards stated in a statement carried by state media that two more oil tankers were on fire in the area.

cards.headline: El Hierro declares emergency amid surge of migrant and refugee arrivals

pages.text: Authorities on El Hierro, one of Spain’s Canary Islands, have declared an emergency and requested assistance from the government in Madrid following a surge of migrants and refugees arriving by boat. Local officials reported that more than 3,300 people have arrived on the island in approximately 30 boats since the start of November. El Hierro has about 11,400 residents. Alpidio Armas, head of the governing council for El Hierro, told Spanish television on November 7, 2026, that the emergency declaration was intended to ensure a framework of cooperation with higher-level institutions due to a sharp increase in arrivals. Armas stated that officials are seeking temporary accommodation for new arrivals and noted that conditions at the island’s hospital have become “undesirable.”

Fernando Clavijo, the regional leader of the Canary Islands, said on November 6, 2026, that the situation is “absolutely unsustainable.” Clavijo noted that arrival numbers are approaching the record levels seen in 2024, with some days reaching a higher pace. To manage the influx, buses have been diverted to migration operations and medical staff have been brought in from other islands. Maritime rescue services rescued 3,261 migrants and refugees off the coast of the Canary Islands during the first six days of November. The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is considered one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Local authorities warned that an approaching storm could increase the danger for migrants currently at sea.

Migration patterns in the region have shifted as increased patrols off the coasts of Senegal, Mauritania, and Morocco have pushed migrants to depart from further south in Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Guinea, resulting in longer, more hazardous crossings. On November 6, 2026, police in Senegal intercepted 142 undocumented migrants, including women and young children, attempting to reach the Canary Islands. This group included 40 Senegalese, 93 Gambians, one national from Guinea-Bissau, two Guineans, and two Nigerians. While irregular migration to the Canary Islands fell by 5.5 percent between January 1 and October 31 compared to the same period previously, recent weeks have seen a significant increase in arrivals.

cards.headline: Paraguay President Santiago Peña placed under house arrest following impeachment

pages.text: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest on November 6, 2026, minutes after Congress impeached him. The arrest follows a banking crisis triggered by the suspension of Ueno bank, which left approximately 60% of the country's adult population—about 2.9 million people—unable to access their bank accounts. Protesters have taken to the streets across the country, with some demonstrations involving violent clashes with police using tear gas and water cannons. Vice-president Pedro Alliana was being sworn in as the new leader while the arrest was ordered. Prosecutor Elena Fiore Franco stated that Peña voluntarily allowed officers to enter his home and made himself available for procedural purposes. The public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into Peña on November 5, 2026, on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering, and influence peddling.

The impeachment proceedings began on November 4, 2026, and concluded on November 6, 2026. During the process, Peña attempted to resign on November 5, 2026, in an effort to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents in Paraguay, who typically become senators for life. However, lawmakers did not accept his resignation, leaving him subject to ordinary courts. Senate president Basilio Núñez stated that Peña was found guilty of dereliction of duty. The impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favor, with one lawmaker absent. Peña, a 47-year-old economist, is being investigated regarding allegations that he used political influence to favor Ueno bank, which expanded exponentially under his government before being suspended due to irregularities. Before the impeachment concluded, Peña posted on social media that he was leaving with gratitude while recognizing the anguish of those waiting for answers.

The crisis involving Ueno bank has left an estimated three million depositors unable to access savings and pensions. On November 3, 2026, long lines of people attempting to withdraw money snaked down the streets of the capital, Asunción. Allegations against Peña include conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds, and participation in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester stated he is due to be questioned over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds. Earlier in his term, Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, a former CEO of Ueno, as head of the country’s central bank. Interim president Pedro Alliana has promised that affected citizens will be fully compensated.

cards.headline: Japan considers early funding for International Criminal Court amid U.S. sanctions

pages.text: Tokyo is considering paying its 2027 contributions to the International Criminal Court (ICC) ahead of schedule, according to government sources. This potential move comes as the court faces sanctions from the United States administration of President Donald Trump. In October, the Trump administration designated the ICC for sanctions and provided a 180-day moratorium. The administration had previously announced sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane in August. If these sanctions are fully implemented as early as April, the ICC could be cut off from dollar-based settlements, which could disrupt operations such as staff salary payments.

cards.headline: Iran shows willingness to discuss nuclear program issues in potential U.S. deal breakthrough

pages.text: The United States and Iran are moving closer to a potential breakthrough in efforts to end the war, as Tehran shows a willingness to discuss issues related to its nuclear program that were previously off the table, according to a diplomat with knowledge of the talks. The diplomat, who asked not to be identified while discussing sensitive information, stated that Iran is studying proposals related to its atomic activities that were presented by chief mediator Qatar. Any concession on these issues could lead to a significant step forward in negotiations, which have been stagnating since the collapse of an interim peace deal agreed in June.

On November 6, 2026, Qatar Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani addressed the difficulty of reaching agreements during a public interview at Oxford University. “We will never have a perfect peace deal but you can’t wait for that perfect moment” Al Thani said, regarding the pursuit of a good deal.

cards.headline: Heavy rains flood approximately 70,000 tents in Gaza Strip

pages.text: Heavy rains from the first winter storm of the season have flooded approximately 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip within 12 hours, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. The flooding has washed away shelters and soaked blankets and mattresses in encampments across the territory. Gaza’s civil defence agency reported receiving about 1,500 distress calls in a 10-hour period after the rain began, noting that water levels in several shelter sites rose by 30-40cm (12-16 inches). While the Government Media Office reported that dozens of walls had collapsed and people had been injured, no fatalities had been reported by the Hamas-run Gaza government media office. Initial losses are estimated at about $3m, according to the Government Media Office. The storm also brought down buildings that had been previously damaged during the war in the enclave that began in October 2023.

Mahmoud Basal, a spokesman for Gaza’s civil defence agency, told Al Jazeera that a few shelter centres were completely flooded, forcing everyone inside them out into the unknown. Basal stated that premature babies, the elderly, and the sick are at the highest risk, adding that those living in tents are at risk of death and illness at any moment. In Gaza City, residents attempted to repair tents, use sand to reinforce them against water, or move children out of flooded shelters. Resident Olfat Magdoub reported being unable to sweep water away from her tent, expressing concern over the impact of future rain. The Government Media Office held Israel “fully responsible” for the situation, citing the continued closure of crossings and the blocking of shelter and reconstruction materials. The office urged UN agencies and the international community to intervene immediately to protect displaced people.

cards.headline: US strikes hit Iran as ship attacks increase in the Strait of Hormuz

pages.text: The United States has bombed Iran following attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators attempt to prevent large-scale fighting between the two nations. On the night of November 6, 2026, two projectiles hit Qeshm, an Iranian island. These strikes are part of a series of air strikes over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defenses and launchers on the southern island. President Donald Trump described the strikes as “minor strikes.”

Maritime activity in the Strait of Hormuz has declined significantly. According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), the week ending November 6 saw 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits, which is approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Most vessels traveling with transponders switched on are using the northern Iranian route. However, many ships are attempting the southern route near Oman with tracking systems offline to shuttle oil out of the waterway. Iranian armed forces claim that tankers and commercial vessels using “unauthorised” routes also risk being hit by naval mines, in addition to missiles and drones.

The UKMTO reported that at least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the week ending November 6, and three of those ships sank. A Western military intelligence agency has recorded 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in early July, though the agency cautioned that most attacks are going unreported. Regarding aerial combat, Iran’s army stated it destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone using an unnamed new system. Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on November 6, 2026, that its air defenses intercepted an MQ-1, which they reported as the 16th aircraft of that model destroyed since the start of the war.

cards.headline: Paraguay's Santiago Peña placed under house arrest following impeachment and bank collapse

pages.text: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest on November 6, 2026, minutes after being impeached by Congress. The leadership change follows the collapse of Ueno Bank, a prominent lender whose suspension left approximately 2.9 million people—about 60% of Paraguay's adult population—unable to access their bank accounts. Pedro Alliana, who previously served as vice president under Peña since 2023, was sworn in as the country's 53rd president on November 6, 2026, to serve until 2028. Alliana promised that affected citizens will be fully compensated and vowed not to abandon those impacted by the financial crisis. Peña, a member of the long-governing Colorado Party, was removed from office after 44 of Paraguay's 45 senators voted in favor of impeachment, with one senator abstaining. Prosecutors ordered the house arrest of the 47-year-old economist on suspicion of breach of trust, illicit enrichment, money laundering, and influence peddling. An arrest warrant was also issued for Carlos Carvallo, the former head of Paraguay's central bank, who is accused of failing in his oversight duties.

The crisis centers on the sudden collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital lender that grew rapidly by offering high returns and generous cash-back offers. The bank's capital fell below the legal minimum, leading the central bank to seize the institution. This collapse left an estimated three million depositors unable to access savings and pensions, and approximately 7,000 employees facing unpaid wages. Investigations have raised questions regarding Peña's potential conflicts of interest, as he held approximately US$1m in shares in a company that became the parent company of Ueno Holding in 2022, which he did not dispose of until April 2025. Additionally, Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo, the former CEO of Ueno, to lead the central bank. While regulating the company he previously ran, Carvallo allowed Ueno to become a digital bank, facilitating its expansion. Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, including money from state pension and health funds. Protests erupted across the country in response to the bank's failure, with some demonstrations on November 5, 2026, involving clashes between protesters and police using tear gas and water cannons.

cards.headline: Tanzanian court sentences opposition leader Tundu Lissu to four years in jail for incitement

pages.text: A High Court in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, has sentenced Tundu Lissu, the leader of the opposition Chadema party, to four years in prison for inciting unrest. The 58-year-old Lissu has been detained since April. While a panel of three judges acquitted him of the more serious charge of treason because prosecutors failed to prove a key element of that charge, they found him guilty of incitement regarding his campaign slogan, “No Reforms, No Election.” The court ruled that by uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, Lissu incited supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election. If the four-year sentence is upheld, it would disqualify Lissu from participating in the next elections due in 2030.

Lissu has denied the charges and described the prosecution as politically motivated. He told the court that the judges manufactured the offence of incitement based on political directives, stating he had only been charged with treason. Lissu noted that applying for bail is possible for an incitement charge, whereas it is not possible for treason. He has been granted leave to appeal the decision at the Court of Appeal, which is Tanzania's highest court.

cards.headline: Inter-American Commission on Human Rights refers Guatemala case to court over violent Indigenous evictions

pages.text: The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) has referred a case to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, asking the court to hold the government of Guatemala responsible and provide reparations for the violent eviction of Indigenous communities. The IACHR announced on Oct. 28 that it submitted the referral to the court, which rules on human rights violations in the Americas, in September. The case concerns 14 Maya Q’eqchi’ communities in Alta Verapaz that were removed from their ancestral land to make way for sugarcane plantations. The IACHR stated that sugarcane cultivation caused displacement and the loss of rice, maize, and bean crops that supported the health and food security of the Maya Q’eqchi’ population, while also substantially affecting the environment.

Disputes in the territory date back to at least 2005, when private companies began buying Indigenous land that the Maya Q’eqchi’ had occupied for centuries, according to the IACHR referral. The government had not granted the communities proper land titles, which created confusion regarding who could occupy the area. In 2011, following years of protests, a court authorized the eviction of the 14 Indigenous communities after residents refused to leave the land. At that time, the government stated it had a “legal and moral obligation to stop the growing number of illegal actions that pose a serious risk to the country’s governability.” The IACHR referral stated the evictions were carried out “violently and with a disproportionate use of force.”

The Commission found that officials failed to research the historical occupation of the land by the communities or the social and cultural impacts that displacement would cause. In May 2013, during the eviction of 95 families on the Río Polochic farm in Panzós, five Indigenous people suffered gunshot wounds and required hospitalization.

cards.headline: UN warns millions fleeing Sudan war face lack of shelter due to funding shortages

pages.text: The United Nations has warned that millions of people fleeing conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter. After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people require emergency shelter and essential household items. However, UN agencies reported they have only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages. Abubakarr Jalloh, the UNHCR deputy representative in Sudan, told reporters that only one third of the $179 million needed to provide shelter has been funded so far. The war, which has raged since April 2023 between the regular army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, has killed more than 200,000 people according to aid worker estimates and has triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.

Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan, stated that out of the targeted group, the agency could reach only 900,000 people. Speaking from Khartoum to reporters in Geneva, Refaat said that while the agency has distributed more than 40,000 tents since the start of the year, their warehouses are now completely empty. He warned that the agency could soon reach a point where families need shelter but nothing remains. Around 8.6 million people remain displaced within Sudan, while millions have fled across borders or returned home to find houses, infrastructure, and essential services damaged or destroyed. In a joint statement, the UNHCR and IOM noted that for those returning home, obtaining shelter is often the first step toward rebuilding lives.

The vulnerability of displaced populations is further compounded by environmental factors. Jalloh stated that three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children. He added that El Niño-related weather conditions have increased vulnerability due to significantly below-average rainfall across the country.

cards.headline: Pakistani astronaut to become first foreign national on China's space station

pages.text: A Pakistani astronaut is scheduled to join the crew of China's Shenzhou 24 spacecraft, a mission that would make him the first foreign national to board Beijing's space station. According to the China Manned Space Agency, reported by the official news agency Xinhua, the astronaut will complete a short on-orbit flight before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft. The mission has not been assigned a specific launch date. This upcoming flight represents the first joint mission involving both Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.

The mission is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025. Two Pakistani candidates, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, have begun training alongside Chinese counterparts. Under the current plan, one of these candidates will be selected as a payload specialist for a short-term spaceflight mission. Training for the candidates has focused on developing hands-on operational capabilities as well as intensive Chinese language instruction.

cards.headline: Police disperse crowd at garment worker’s gayebana janaza in Gazipur, Bangladesh

pages.text: Police clashed with National Citizen Party (NCP) activists at Chandana Chowrasta on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway in Gazipur, Bangladesh, during a gayebana janaza—a funeral prayer for someone believed to be in good standing with their faith—for garment worker Toufique Hossain. The prayer was organized by NCP and Sramik Shakti leaders under the banner of 'Workers-Students-People.' According to reports, police arrived toward the end of the program and requested that organizers clear the road, leading to an altercation involving pushing and shoving as leaders urged police to allow the prayer to continue. NCP Central Chief Organiser Advocate Ali Nasher alleged that police beat activists with batons and fired at least four sound grenades to disperse the crowd, resulting in at least 20 injuries. Basan Police Station OC Mohammad Harun Rashid stated he knew nothing about the incident, while District Executive Magistrate Arif Hossain said the administration was discouraging public meetings and gatherings due to the current situation.

Toufique Hossain, 35, died on November 6, 2026, while undergoing treatment at Shin Shin Japan Hospital in Uttara, Dhaka. He had been injured during an ongoing labor movement in Gazipur involving demands for a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000. Hossain, who lived in the Banglabazar area of Gazipur and hailed from Gobindaganj upazila of Gaibandha, worked in the cutting section of Layla Styles Limited. During the funeral prayer, speakers stated the event was a religious observance rather than a provocative program and noted that Hossain's body had been buried in haste. Organizers also demanded that authorities resolve workers' demands within three days, stop the arrest and harassment of workers, and release those already detained.

cards.headline: US carries out round of “minor” strikes on Iran, Trump says

pages.text: President Donald Trump said the US military carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran on November 6, 2026, targeting an air defence system. Trump described the action as “minor,” telling reporters that the military knocked out an anti-aircraft device in approximately five to 15 minutes. Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, located in the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the US war on Iran began in February. These strikes follow previous US military reports of “defensive” strikes on November 2, 2026, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

The military actions occur as Trump's administration navigates diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. On November 6, 2026, Trump stated that the US has been talking to Iran and that progress has been made, though he has also vacillated between suggesting a resolution is near and threatening to “destroy” Iran. On November 12, 2026, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts. Differences regarding Iran's nuclear program remain a central issue that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any potential deal. US Central Command announced on X that the US is offering a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information regarding Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel through the State Department’s Rewards for Justice program.

The strikes come after the Republican party faced a significant defeat in US midterm elections, a setback partially attributed to voter dissatisfaction with the Iran war and resulting elevated fuel prices. Majed al-Ansari, spokesperson for the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, dismissed claims on X that negotiations between the US and Iran had failed, stating such claims only benefit those seeking to prolong the war. Observers note that Iran's demands regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, balanced against the political pressure on Trump following the midterms, create a difficult situation for the US president.

cards.headline: Former firefighter provides life-saving aid after bus crash near Mackenzie, B.C.

pages.text: Rich Rogers, a former City of Prince George firefighter, provided immediate medical treatment to passengers following a bus crash on Highway 39, just south of Mackenzie, British Columbia. Rogers, who had previously left firefighting due to mental health concerns, was traveling with his wife, Corynn, and their son when the bus drove toward their vehicle and crashed into a ditch. At the time of the crash, Rogers' family were the only other people on the desolate highway. While Corynn Rogers attempted to call 911 in an area with poor cell coverage, Rich Rogers ran down a steep bank to the bus. He turned off the vehicle as it was filling with gas, checked for pulses, and revived unconscious passengers. His wife stated that he literally saved several lives.

The crash resulted in up to 20 people requiring urgent care. The emergency response included six ambulances, five airplanes, and a helicopter. A Code Orange—an emergency protocol used to manage a sudden influx of patients—was declared at hospitals in both Mackenzie and Prince George, which is approximately 200 kilometres south of the scene. Following the incident, 15 patients were released, while 5 remained hospitalized. The experience reopened the mental trauma Rogers had sought to leave behind when he exited his firefighting career. Rogers, who moved to Mackenzie in September, requested to conduct a single interview via online video call to discuss the impact such situations have on those who provide help and the necessity of supporting first responders.

cards.headline: Ghana loses an estimated $6.56 billion in annual potential mining revenue

pages.text: Ghana loses an estimated $6.56 billion in potential revenue from its mining sector every year because the government has limited participation in mineral extraction, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS). At a policy briefing in Accra on November 6, 2026, IFS Executive Director Dr. Said Boakye stated that the country is unable to maximize returns from its mineral resources. He urged authorities to use the upcoming 2027 Budget to address this leakage. Dr. Boakye attributed the stronger performance of Botswana to that country's active involvement in mining through partnerships with private companies. In 2025, Botswana generated $13.4 billion in value added from mining, while Ghana's revenue from the sector was $1.6 billion, representing 11.9 per cent of the sector's value. Dr. Boakye noted that if Ghana had generated mining revenue at Botswana's average rate of 60.9 per cent, the government would have earned $8.16 billion instead of the $1.6 billion collected.

The IFS report also highlighted broader issues with domestic revenue mobilization in Ghana. Dr. Boakye identified tax evasion, underreporting, tax avoidance, and collusion involving revenue administrators as major factors undermining revenue collection. He noted that low revenue mobilization has constrained the country's ability to finance development. In April 2026, Ghana Revenue Authority Commissioner-General Anthony Sarpong revealed that the country lost more than GH¢11 billion in revenue at its ports due to incorrect declarations regarding the valuation, classification, and country of origin of imported goods. Regarding broader economic metrics, the IFS reported that Ghana's total revenue and grants-to-GDP ratio was 15.7 per cent in 2022, compared to an average of 20.1 per cent for 25 sub-Saharan African countries examined in the report. This placed Ghana 18th among those 25 countries. The IFS estimated that if Ghana's revenue-to-GDP ratio had matched the sub-Saharan African average, it would have collected GH¢288.26 billion in total revenue and grants in 2025, rather than the actual collection of GH¢224.88 billion.

cards.headline: Israeli forces abduct olive picker and restrict access to more than half of Deir Mimas farmland

pages.text: Israeli forces opened fire near a group of residents and abducted one person while they were harvesting olives on the outskirts of Deir Mimas, according to mayor Tania Barnaba. The mayor told The National that the group was picking olives in an area that had been designated as off-limits. Following the incident, Israeli troops established a checkpoint on the outskirts of the village, which has blocked further access to the olive groves. These restrictions have rendered more than half of the southern Lebanese village’s olive groves inaccessible to residents. Deir Mimas is almost entirely dependent on olive cultivation and olive oil production for the income of many residents.

The village has been informed that it falls within the Israeli military's so-called “yellow line,” a boundary that separates areas of southern Lebanon under Lebanese state control from areas occupied by Israel where Israeli troops restrict civilian access. Mayor Barnaba stated that the village found itself inside this line without any formal marking or explanation. She noted that residents learned of this status following a confrontation between Israeli forces and the Lebanese Armed Forces in mid-September. On September 18, Israeli troops approached a newly established Lebanese army observation post near the village and threw stun grenades in its vicinity, which prompted the army to withdraw to its main post in the town. The restrictions occur within or near Israel’s “security zone,” a territory approximately 10-12km deep that is occupied by Israel.

cards.headline: Soil contamination and low regulatory compliance pose risks in Ghana's Savannah Region mining communities

pages.text: Three baseline studies on artisanal and small-scale gold mining in the Savannah Region of Ghana have revealed widespread soil contamination, low regulatory compliance, and weak institutional coordination. Conducted under the European Union-funded Gold for Good (G4G) Project, the assessments identified significant environmental and health risks for communities in the West Gonja Municipality, Bole District, and Sawla-Tuna-Kalba District. The studies found that 68.64 per cent of mapped mining areas fell within a critical environmental-risk category, with contaminated soil identified as the dominant pathway for exposure to toxins.

Environmental sampling showed that cadmium levels exceeded international guideline values in all soil samples, while mercury levels were above recommended thresholds in approximately 94 per cent of the samples. Cadmium accounted for more than three-quarters of the assessed health hazard, though mercury exposure and dust inhalation were also identified as major risks. Regarding health impacts, about 46 per cent of children’s exposure scenarios exceeded acceptable non-carcinogenic health-risk thresholds, compared with 20 per cent for adults. Women faced increased exposure due to their involvement in ore processing and handling contaminated materials, while children were vulnerable through contact with polluted soil and proximity to residential gold-processing sites.

The research, which drew on a survey of 953 respondents across 30 communities and the mapping of 94 mining sites, also highlighted gaps in mining formalization and oversight. Only 2.92 per cent of respondents held mining licences, 15.96 per cent had registered land, and about 74 per cent were unaware of the regulations governing mining in their communities. Additionally, 98.33 per cent of gold transactions were conducted in cash, which the studies noted raises concerns regarding traceability and oversight.

cards.headline: Seven Montreal police officers fired amid misconduct scandal

pages.text: The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) has fired seven officers in what is described as an unprecedented move. This action follows a months-long misconduct scandal involving allegations of racism, discrimination, criminal misconduct, and the mistreatment of vulnerable people within the force. Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher has responded to the scandal by appearing in media interviews and before reporters, promising consequences for officers found to have committed wrongdoing and placing transparency at the center of his public response.

Despite the firings, researchers and community advocates have raised questions regarding the force's response. Daniele-Jocelyne Otou, executive director of Montreal’s Black Healing Centre and co-founder of New Room, stated that while the force is effective at transparency as part of public relations, she believes they skirt around true accountability. Advocates argue that punishing individual officers and making misconduct public may not address the underlying conditions that allowed the alleged behavior to occur.

Ricardo Lamour, a community worker, human rights advocate, and former fellow of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights program in Geneva, criticized the response as a push to control the narrative. Lamour suggested the response should be viewed alongside Chief Dagher's public image of being close to Montreal communities, stating that this “proximity brand is cracking.” He believes the chief and the mayor are presenting a shared narrative of “a reforming chief against a resistant culture.”

cards.headline: Documentary explores the restoration of cultural heritage in Mosul, Iraq

pages.text: The documentary film *The Lions by the River Tigris*, directed by Zaradasht Ahmed, examines the efforts to revive the beauty of Mosul, Iraq, following the city's devastation after its liberation from ISIL (ISIS). The film focuses on the city's 8,000-year history and a quiet cultural revival occurring as Mosul rebuilds. Central to the narrative are two carved lions on a marble gate that serve as a link to the city's past amidst the war-ravaged landscape.

The film follows the stories of three men in Mosul. Bashar, a fisherman, guards a marble gate crowned with lions, which is all that remains of his once-grand family home lost during the battle to liberate the city from ISIL nearly 10 years ago. Fakhri, a collector seeking to save Mosul’s heritage, is depicted as becoming obsessed with acquiring the lions gate for his unofficial museum. Fakhri's friend Fadil, a musician who was once silenced under ISIL, challenges him to recognize the human cost associated with every artefact.

cards.headline: Canada's youth-focused roster debuts at Women's Ice Hockey World Championship in Denmark

pages.text: Canada opened its IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship campaign with a 5-1 victory over Sweden in Denmark. The 11-day tournament features 10 nations, with Canada and the U.S. considered the favorites. Canada has won 13 world titles, while the U.S. has won 11 of the previous 24 championships. Canada's next scheduled game is against Japan. This tournament follows a period of transition for the team, as captain and hockey icon Marie-Philip Poulin is sidelined due to knee surgery after tearing her ACL last spring, marking the first time in more than a decade the team has played without her.

The Canadian roster is notably young, with an average age of 26 years, two months, and 22 days. According to Hockey Canada, this is the youngest roster the country has fielded at the Women's Worlds since 2013. The team includes seven players making their world championship debuts, including 18-year-olds Rosalie Tremblay and Hayley McDonald, and 19-year-old Sara Manness. Three collegiate players are returning for their second world championship: 19-year-old Chloe Primerano of the University of Minnesota, and 20-year-old Caitlin Kraemer and 23-year-old Ève Gascon, both of the University of Minnesota Duluth. The oldest player on the roster is 32-year-old goaltender Ann-Renée Desbien.

cards.headline: Evacuation order issued for Zeballos, British Columbia, following landslide and flooding

pages.text: An evacuation order has been issued for Zeballos, a village of approximately 125 people on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island, due to risks from flooding and landslides. The village has also declared a state of local emergency. Emergency Info B.C. stated there is a potential risk to life and safety, and anyone in the order area must evacuate immediately. The Ministry of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness reported that a landslide occurred in the village overnight. Ehattesaht First Nation Chief Simon John said heavy rain began in the middle of the night and flooding started in the early morning.

The Strathcona Regional District reported that debris from a landslide has affected the area. According to the district, it remains unclear whether further landslides are possible until a geotechnical assessment—an evaluation of the earth's stability and soil conditions—is completed. The district stated that monitoring and assessment activities are continuing. A rainfall warning has been issued for parts of Vancouver Island and Metro Vancouver, and the Strathcona Regional District's emergency operations centre has been activated.

The evacuation order affects 22 properties on Pandora Crescent and Maquinna Avenue, according to the Strathcona Regional District. An evacuation alert, which advises residents to be ready to leave, covers three addresses on Ferris Road. Residents in the area of Pandora, Gold Valley, and Reno roads are encouraged to shelter in place and remain in their homes. The Strathcona Regional District said on its website that public safety remains the priority and that it will provide updates as more information becomes available.

cards.headline: Wind gusts exceeding 100 km/h cause power outages and road closures in Prince George and Central Interior

pages.text: Wind gusts recorded at more than 100 km/h caused widespread disruption across Prince George, British Columbia, and the wider Central Interior on the night of November 6, 2026. The high winds knocked down trees, which in turn closed roads and damaged power lines. Environment Canada data showed ongoing gusts between 94 and 102 km/h from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m. local time, with sustained wind speeds ranging from 41 to 61 km/h. Social media reports included images of trees on homes and a missing traffic light.

The damage left roughly 23,000 customers in the region without power, including those in 100 Mile House, Williams Lake, Quesnel, and Vanderhoof. At one point, approximately one-third of the city of Prince George was without electricity. Hydro outage maps from 11 p.m. indicated that tens of thousands of customers were also without power throughout Vancouver Island. The power provider asked for patience as crews worked to restore service under challenging conditions.

Emergency responders addressed multiple incidents, including several small fires sparked by damaged power lines. In rural neighbourhoods, volunteer firefighting groups urged residents to stay inside. The District of Vanderhoof warned residents to stay clear of fallen power lines or anything touching them, stating all downed lines should be treated as live. Hydro advised people to stay at least 10 metres away from any sagging or downed power lines and to report such incidents to 911.

cards.headline: Expatriates fund 100 streetlights for Sonalia village in Tangail, Bangladesh

pages.text: Expatriates from Sonalia village in Tangail’s Basail upazila have funded the installation of 100 streetlights to illuminate a three-kilometre stretch from Karatia Bazar to the Sonalia graveyard. The initiative, named “Alokito Sonalia” (Illuminated Sonalia), was completed in five months at a cost of Tk 10 lakh. The lights remain on from dusk until dawn, providing visibility for a road that previously caused villagers to struggle at night. Before the installation, students faced difficulties attending evening coaching classes, women felt unsafe, and thefts were common in the area.

The project was implemented by a committee formed by villagers working abroad, including more than 100 young men working in Singapore and others living in Europe and the United States. Amir Ali, a village resident who works as a factory worker in Woodlands Industrial Park, Singapore, stated that the group spent between Tk 7,000 and Tk 8,000 for each light, which were installed every 100 feet. Ali noted that the committee members contributed their own money to the project. Beyond the streetlights, these expatriates have spent the past two years building a road to the graveyard, planting flower gardens, constructing houses for the poor, and distributing Eid gifts to 200 households.

cards.headline: Maasai communities in southern Kenya face water shortages following mine closure

pages.text: The temporary shutdown of a major trona ore mine in southern Kenya has left approximately 30,000 Maasai people without their primary water supply. For decades, the mine operator provided water to the remote region in addition to employment. Following a temporary shutdown by the Kenyan government amid a controversial contract dispute, the water supply for the Maasai largely dried up. Many community members must now walk for hours to collect water, and limited water deliveries to the communities have fallen far short of meeting their significant needs.

The mine, located near Lake Magadi, has been operated by the Indian conglomerate Tata Chemicals for over a century. The company extracts trona ore—a mineral used to process glass and cleaning products—from the lake for export. The current water crisis follows the Kenyan government's decision to temporarily close the mine during a dispute regarding its contract.

cards.headline: Thirteen Adivasi families face delayed resettlement following Wayanad landslides

pages.text: Thirteen Adivasi families displaced by the 2024 Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide in Kerala remain without permanent housing as resettlement efforts continue. While 327 families, including 149, have been allotted houses at a township project in Kalpetta, these 13 families face a different situation because their original homes were not damaged, but the surrounding areas were designated as “no-go zones” unsuitable for habitation. One of these settlements was also classified as a “red zone.” Due to these designations, some of these families are living in rented accommodation with government assistance, which has separated them from their traditional livelihoods and forest environment. Other families have returned to the forest because construction has not yet begun on promised houses at Puthiyavillage in Meppadi. cards.headline: Severe acute malnutrition in children rising across Sudan amid war and climate change

pages.text: War, poverty, and climate change are driving an increase in child malnutrition in Sudan. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) estimates that 825,000 children under the age of five will suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, which represents a 7 percent increase from 2025. This crisis occurs as a civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary has continued since April 2023.

In the first six months of the year, UNICEF and its partners treated 174,700 children with severe acute malnutrition nationwide. In Port Sudan, the Port Sudan Teaching Hospital recorded 433 cases between January and August. One case involved five-year-old Adam, who was brought to the hospital by his mother, Layla Ali, after a two-and-a-half-hour journey from the village of al-Lalouba. Ali reported that Adam's malnutrition left his ribs visibly protruding and that he had become too sick to move after losing his appetite two weeks prior. Ali stated that the distance to the hospital and concerns regarding treatment costs initially prevented her from seeking medical help, but she sought care when his condition deteriorated. Adam spent five days in the hospital receiving treatment for recurring bouts of malnutrition.

cards.headline: More than 230 migrant workers in Singapore connected with potential employers

pages.text: More than 230 migrant workers in Singapore have been connected with potential employers and placed in temporary housing while their salary claims, which were lodged in October, remain pending. During a job-matching exercise held Nov 6 at the Ministry of Manpower’s (MOM) onboarding centre for migrant workers in Sengkang West, workers were interviewed by construction and process firms. Md Sabbir Alam, a 23-year-old worker for Process Maintenance Solutions and the sole breadwinner for a family of four in Bangladesh, said he was paid his wages in early November. cards.headline: Stanford University researchers create 'alien-cortical' mice with human brain cells

pages.text: Researchers at Stanford University in California, United States, have developed mice containing millions of working human neurons. According to a study published in Nature, these so-called “alien-cortical mice” may provide a new method for studying neural circuits and brain disorders, including dementia, cerebral palsy, and schizophrenia. The development has ignited debates regarding the future of cross-species medical research and the nature of neurohybrids.

To create the mice, researchers genetically modified them so they were born and grew without most of the hippocampus and the cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex is the outer region of the brain that plays a major role in decision-making, attention, movement, and perception. The hippocampus is a brain structure needed for memory and learning. When the mice were two days old, researchers injected human organoids into the resulting empty spaces in their brains. Organoids are miniature masses of cells grown in a laboratory from tumor tissue or stem cells that mimic real human organs.

Each human organoid used in the study was grown from the stem cells of healthy donors and contained approximately 100,000 human cells. In the overall process, researchers removed about 14 million mouse neurons and added about 4 million human neurons.

cards.headline: Light-powered reaction transforms difficult-to-repurpose sulfonamides into drug building blocks

pages.text: Researchers at Florida State University have developed a light-powered chemical reaction capable of transforming sulfonamides into useful building blocks for future drug discovery. This method provides a way to repurpose a class of compounds that are typically considered chemical ``dead ends'' because they are difficult to modify. During the drug development process, which can take a decade or more, tens of thousands of chemical compounds are produced that never become medicines; this new technique aims to give some of those compounds a second chance at becoming the foundation for drugs. The research was published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society by assistant professor of chemistry and biochemistry Bryan Kudisch and his collaborators.

Sulfonamides are a critical molecular substructure in medicinal chemistry, appearing in the name of the ``sulfa drugs'' that were among the first widely used antibiotics nearly 90 years ago. While they remain essential to medicines treating conditions such as HIV, melanoma, high blood pressure, and type 2 diabetes, they are notoriously difficult to repurpose. This difficulty stems from the fact that sulfonamides are chemically inert. While chemists have established methods to interconvert many other functional groups to change a compound's biological properties, few options exist for sulfonamides, particularly regarding the sulfur atom at the center of these substructures. Kudisch, a molecular spectroscopist who uses laser-based techniques to measure short-time processes induced by light, led the team in developing this light-driven transformation.

cards.headline: Exposure to 'high safety' plasticizer DINCH linked to lower birth weight and fetal complications

pages.text: A peer-reviewed study from New York University Langone Health suggests that exposure to DINCH, a chemical used in plastic food packaging, is linked to lower birth weights, shorter birth lengths, and fetal development complications. These complications can increase the risk of heart disease, obesity, and learning difficulties that may persist into adolescence and adulthood, according to the study authors. DINCH, formally named 1,2-cyclohexane dicarboxylic acid diisononyl ester, is a plasticizer used to make plastic more flexible and durable. It is found in products such as cling film, plastic wine corks, children’s toys, medical devices, textiles, and flooring. While industry has marketed DINCH as a “high safety,” nontoxic alternative to common phthalate plasticizers, this analysis of US federal health data suggests it may not be as safe as claimed.

Researchers analyzed data from over 6,600 pregnancies collected through the National Institutes of Health Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (Echo) Program. The study found that up to 70% of women showed DINCH in their urine. Higher levels of the chemical were associated with an increased risk of a child being classified as “small for gestational age,” which means the baby is below the 10th percentile for babies born at the same stage of pregnancy. Although research into the health risks of DINCH is limited, existing evidence suggests the chemicals may act as hormone disruptors that impact child development. Leonardo Trasande, a lead author of the NYU paper, stated that chemicals should be properly tested for safety before they become a widespread exposure for the general public.

cards.headline: Protein analysis reveals all Homo naledi remains found so far are female

pages.text: A protein analysis of at least 20 individuals of the ancient human species Homo naledi has revealed that all identified remains are female. By extracting proteins from tooth enamel, researchers found the specimens appear to be missing the Y chromosome, which is the genetic marker for males. This finding adds a new layer of mystery to the species, which lived in South Africa between approximately 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, around the same time early modern humans emerged. All remains discovered to date have been located within the Rising Star Cave system in the Cradle of Humankind, South Africa.

The Homo naledi fossils were first discovered in 2013 by two cavers exploring the Rising Star Cave system. In 2015, the remains were described as a new species. In 2016, at least three additional individuals were found in another chamber of the cave, but no remains have been found outside of this specific location. Although Homo naledi lived alongside the earliest modern humans (Homo sapiens), the species is anatomically archaic and more similar to earlier hominins such as Australopithecus and H. habilis. Researchers remain puzzled by how so many remains ended up in a tight, difficult-to-access cave system.

There is ongoing disagreement regarding how the remains reached the cave. Palaeoanthropologist Lee Berger, who named the species in 2015 and is a co-author of the recent study published in the journal Cell, argues that the bodies may have been deliberately carried and placed in the chamber. Berger told Science that the absence of males suggests Homo naledi may have engaged in cultural behavior that separates males and females in death rituals. However, other researchers discount claims of intentional burial, suggesting instead that natural forces deposited the bodies together.

cards.headline: Robotic builder completes first autonomous structure assembly in space

pages.text: A robotic truss builder designed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) has successfully constructed a structure in space without astronaut assistance for the first time. The demonstration, known as the Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA), involved a robot working for six months to build a 1.4-meter-diameter (4.6-foot-diameter) reflector antenna using aluminum joints, composite fiber tubes, and a Kapton reflective surface. While the team encountered time limitations and only completed the initial section of the antenna, the demonstration confirmed the feasibility of an assembly concept that could be scaled to support much larger perimeter trusses and giant reflective surfaces.

The ASTRA demonstration is the third phase of a project under DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program. In the first two phases, the ASTRA team developed the design methodology and verified the concept in Earth-based laboratory settings. The space payload was completed, tested, and delivered to the payload host, Momentus Inc., in less than 12 months. The robotic builder utilizes an autonomous manipulator to pick up struts and joints from nearby dispensers to repeatedly assemble identical sections, or bays, of a perimeter truss.

Sergio Pellegrino, a senior research scientist at JPL and team leader of the ASTRA demonstration, described the achievement as the first time a structure has been autonomously constructed in space. Pellegrino, who also serves as co-director of the Space Solar Power Project—an initiative aiming to harvest solar power in space and wirelessly transmit it to Earth—noted that developing such a complex payload on a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for the small team.
